issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of natural disaster and with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes alarm/reactivity and fragmented recall rather than interpersonal domination or coercion. For this trauma type, this item introduces an implausible trigger theme not supported elsewhere in threat, memory, or appraisals.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
issues.explanation: Avoiding hospitals/ambulances/physical examinations is not well supported by the rest of the profile for a natural-disaster trauma. There are no memory or threat items involving injury treatment, medical rescue, or bodily harm, so this strategy appears to target a symptom theme not represented elsewhere. In contrast, the profile is centered on generalized alarm, shouting, unpredictability, and fragmented memory.

issues.item: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
issues.explanation: Self-harm is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context: the other selected items describe a classic hyperarousal/re-experiencing natural-disaster PTSD presentation with avoidance and overeating, but no accompanying items suggest the kind of shame, self-punitive appraisal, dissociative affect regulation, or broader emotion-dysregulation pattern that would make physical self-harm clinically coherent here. It stands out as addressing a symptom process not otherwise represented in the five components.

Alcohol smell is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly anchored to the reported trauma type and the rest of the item set. The other triggers (unpredictability, shouting) fit a danger/hyperarousal formulation, whereas alcohol smell implies a very specific sensory trauma cue that is not supported by the memory or threat items. Given a natural-disaster index trauma, this trigger is difficult to explain clinically without additional corroborating content.

vignette: John, a 55-year-old African American bomb disposal technician married to his high school sweetheart, was profoundly affected by the natural disaster that occurred six months ago. The event, a devastating tornado, not only swept through his neighborhood but also triggered memories of his military service and bomb disposal operations. On the day of the tornado, John was at home when he heard a sudden loud roar outside. He immediately recognized it as something dangerous. As he rushed to secure his family, the unpredictable nature of the event left him in constant fear for their lives. The moment the sirens began to wail and shouting could be heard from neighbors, his body reacted before he had time to think. He found himself diving into a safe room, his heart racing as if he were back in combat. Since then, John has been plagued by unpredictable situations that trigger intense flashbacks and false alarms. Any loud noise or sudden shout can send him spiraling into panic, reliving the chaos of the tornado. This unpredictability exacerbates his sense of danger; his body reacts as though he is still under threat even when there's no real peril. To cope with this distress, John often turns to maladaptive strategies. He eats excessively to numb his emotions and avoids anything that could be stressful. His need for mental distraction keeps him constantly occupied, often working late into the night on trivial tasks. However, these behaviors only serve to heighten his triggers. The more he isolates himself or distracts himself with food and work, the more he remains hyper-vigilant to any sudden noise or unpredictable event. John's memory of the tornado is fragmented and incomplete. He finds himself pushing away the full recall before it can settle, leaving him with only bits and pieces that feel like a puzzle without an answer. When he does manage to remember parts of what happened, intense rage surges through him, fueling his false alarms and making him react as though danger is imminent. The cycle tightens further when John recalls the event, igniting both his sense of threat and his triggers. The fragmented memories and intense emotions trigger more frequent false alarms and flashbacks, leading to a heightened state of arousal that only exacerbates his maladaptive coping mechanisms. He often overeats or avoids social gatherings, pushing himself deeper into isolation. Despite these efforts to manage his distress, John's life has become increasingly difficult. His work as a bomb disposal technician requires him to be in unpredictable and potentially dangerous situations daily. The unpredictability of his job now triggers intense reactions that interfere with his ability to perform tasks safely and effectively. His wife notices the changes too; he is often distant and irritable, struggling to connect emotionally. What finally brought John to seek help was a near-miss incident at work where his heightened state of arousal led him to misjudge a situation critically. He realized that if he didn't get help soon, he would either lose his job or worse, put himself and others in grave danger. John is most afraid of losing control again-of being unable to predict when the next false alarm will strike and how it might affect those around him. Yet, he hopes for a way to regain a sense of calm and stability, to be able to face unpredictable situations without feeling like his body is reacting out of control. He dreams of a day when he can return to work without fear, and more importantly, connect with his family in a meaningful way again.
